milestones.title: do the quoted words exist?
milestones.task: Write normalise_with_map(text) returning (norm, idx), verify_quote(quote, passage) returning the (start, end) span in the original passage or None, and check_citation(cite, corpus) returning "no_such_source", "quote_not_found" or "ok". The character table _QUOTE_MAP and split_fragments are given.
milestones.checkpoint: python3 check.py shows this milestone as ✔. It checks hand-worked normalisations (including the double space, a newline-and-tab run, curly quotes and a non-breaking space), exact quotations with and without the full stop, messy case and whitespace, the ellipsis in both forms, fragments out of order, the same words used twice, one changed figure, empty and too-short quotations, a curly apostrophe against a straight one; sixty seeded quotations cut from the handbook and mangled (each must be found, and its span must normalise to the quotation) with one word broken (each must be rejected); and then every citation of the dev set against the status the generator planted.
milestones.explain:
The cheapest checks come first because they catch the most embarrassing failures at almost no cost. A citation is a pair: a document identifier and a quotation. Two questions need no model at all. Is there a document with that identifier? And does the quotation occur in it? If the answer to either is no, nothing else about the citation matters, and a fabricated reference (the failure of Fake Citations in Court) is stopped by a dictionary lookup.

Matching a quotation against a document sounds like quote in text, and it nearly is. Three details turn it into real work. First, models and people copy loosely: they change case, collapse a line break into a space, turn a curly apostrophe into a straight one. A check that rejects those would block honest quotations, so both sides are normalised before comparing: lower-cased, with quotes, dashes and non-breaking spaces replaced by their plain forms and each run of whitespace collapsed to one space. (Normalisation is a security topic too: Injection & Untrusted Input explains why canonical forms matter whenever text is compared.) Second, you want to show the reader where the quotation sits, to highlight it or to log which span backed the claim, and that span must be in the original document, not in the normalised copy. So normalisation has to remember where each character came from.

Third, quotations have gaps. A model that wants to quote half a sentence writes "Adult entry ... costs 14 pounds", and the ellipsis means that words were left out. The honest reading is that the fragments must occur in order, each after the end of the previous one. Allowing them to overlap or go backwards would accept a quotation assembled from the same four words used twice. A fourth detail guards against the opposite error: a quotation of one or two words ("14 pounds") occurs somewhere in nearly every document by chance and proves nothing, so a quotation whose fragments total fewer than MIN_QUOTE_CHARS (12) characters is rejected.

A short script on the first document shows the behaviour you are aiming for (it uses the finished functions; swap solution for starter once yours passes):

from solution import *

passage = CORPUS["D01"]
print(passage, "\n")
for q in ["capacity for 300 visitors",
          "CAPACITY  for 300\nvisitors.",
          "Adult entry ... costs 14 pounds",
          "costs 14 pounds ... Adult entry",
          "capacity for 301 visitors",
          "14 pounds"]:
    span = verify_quote(q, passage)
    print(f"{q!r:36} -> {span}", repr(passage[span[0]:span[1]]) if span else "")
print()
print(normalise_with_map("It’s  a   fee"))
Marlow Pool has capacity for 300 visitors. Adult entry to Marlow Pool costs 14 pounds. Marlow Pool opened in 1983. Marlow Pool closes at 9 pm on weekdays. 

'capacity for 300 visitors'          -> (16, 41) 'capacity for 300 visitors'
'CAPACITY  for 300\nvisitors.'       -> (16, 42) 'capacity for 300 visitors.'
'Adult entry ... costs 14 pounds'    -> (43, 85) 'Adult entry to Marlow Pool costs 14 pounds'
'costs 14 pounds ... Adult entry'    -> None 
'capacity for 301 visitors'          -> None 
'14 pounds'                          -> None 

("it's a fee", [0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 7, 10, 11, 12])

The last line is the map for "It’s a fee": the straight apostrophe replaces the curly one, the runs of spaces become single spaces, and each space points at the first space of its run.

Common misconception

"The quotation is in the document, so the citation is fine." The quotation check proves the words exist and nothing more. Answer A0005 above quotes a real sentence from a real document, about a different venue. The check you are writing here answers "did the model make this up?", not "does this source say what the sentence says?". Mixing the two up is how teams ship a citation checker that reports 95% and a product that is still wrong a third of the time.

milestones.title: does the cited text support the claim?
milestones.task: Write judge_claim(claim, passages) returning Verdict(label, score, sentence) by the five rules above, and evaluate_judge(items, judge=None) returning confusion (a dict with all nine (gold, predicted) pairs), accuracy, precision and recall of SUPPORTED (each 1.0 when its denominator is zero) and false_support (the (claim, gold) pairs wrongly approved, in input order). The helpers words_of, numbers_of, has_negation and split_sentences are given.
milestones.checkpoint: python3 check.py shows this milestone as ✔. It checks hand-worked claims (a synonym, a changed number, a missing document, the two-of-five-words case, exactly 0.6 which must pass, a negation in the evidence, 3,200 against 3200, no passages, a claim of stop words only), a stub judge for evaluate_judge, and then the label and score of every claim in the dev set and in 200 test answers against an independent re-implementation of the rules, before it checks precision and recall on the dev set.
milestones.explain:
A quotation can be real and irrelevant. The question that matters is whether the cited text entails the claim: if the passage is true, must the claim be true? Models that answer this are doing natural language inference, with three labels (SUPPORTED, CONTRADICTED, NOT_ENOUGH_INFO), exactly as in chapter 12. Here the judge is a small rule-based stand-in so that the lab runs offline and you can read every decision. Its rules are those of the chapter's verifier:

  1. Split the cited documents into sentences, and each claim and sentence into content words (words_of: letters only, no stop words, synonyms folded, so "can hold" and "has capacity for" meet). Numbers are handled separately (numbers_of).
  2. For each sentence, overlap is the share of the claim's content words that the sentence contains. The best sentence is the one with the highest overlap (the first on a tie).
  3. If the best overlap is below MIN_OVERLAP (0.6), nothing in the text addresses the claim: NOT_ENOUGH_INFO.
  4. If one side contains a negation ("not", "no", "never") and the other does not, the text says the opposite: CONTRADICTED.
  5. If the claim contains a number that the best sentence does not, it states a different figure: CONTRADICTED. Otherwise SUPPORTED.

The score of a verdict is the overlap, whatever the label; you will use it in milestone 3. Two claims against the first document ("Marlow Pool has capacity for 300 visitors. Adult entry to Marlow Pool costs 14 pounds. ..."): "Marlow Pool can hold 300 visitors." has all four content words in the first sentence, so it is SUPPORTED with score 1.0; "Marlow Pool can hold 250 visitors." has the same words and a different number, so it is CONTRADICTED. "Marlow Pool has 40 car parking spaces." shares only the venue name with any sentence (2 of 5 words, 0.4), so it is NOT_ENOUGH_INFO.

The rules are simple on purpose, and every rule has a way to fail. That is the point of the second half of the milestone: evaluate_judge scores a judge against gold labels and returns the confusion matrix, the accuracy, and two numbers that matter more than accuracy. Precision of SUPPORTED is the share of claims the judge approves that really are supported; its complement is the false-support rate, the dangerous error because it stamps a wrong claim as checked. Recall of SUPPORTED is the share of supported claims it approves; its complement is the share of good answers it needlessly vetoes. Here is the finished judge on the claims of the dev set:

from solution import *

def claim_items(answers):
    out = []
    for a in answers:
        for s in a["statements"]:
            texts = [CORPUS[c["doc"]] for c in s["cites"] if c["doc"] in CORPUS]
            if texts:
                out.append((s["text"], texts, s["gold"]))
    return out

items = claim_items(dev_set())
r = evaluate_judge(items)
short = {"SUPPORTED": "SUP", "CONTRADICTED": "CON", "NOT_ENOUGH_INFO": "NEI"}
print("rows = gold, columns = predicted:    SUP  CON  NEI")
for g in LABELS:
    print(f"  {g:<16}" + "".join(f"{r['confusion'][(g, p)]:>9}" for p in LABELS))
print(f"accuracy {r['accuracy']:.3f}  precision of SUPPORTED {r['precision']:.3f}  recall {r['recall']:.3f}\n")
print("claims judged SUPPORTED that are not:")
for claim, gold in r["false_support"]:
    print(f"  [{short[gold]}] {claim}")
print("\nMIN_OVERLAP sweep (dev set):")
import solution
for t in (0.4, 0.5, 0.6, 0.7, 0.8, 0.9):
    solution.MIN_OVERLAP = t
    r = evaluate_judge(items)
    print(f"  {t:.1f}  accuracy {r['accuracy']:.3f}  precision {r['precision']:.3f}  recall {r['recall']:.3f}  false supports {len(r['false_support'])}")

  CONTRADICTED            0       14        0
  NOT_ENOUGH_INFO         5        5       16

  0.8  accuracy 0.923  precision 0.964  recall 0.931  false supports 4
  0.9  accuracy 0.859  precision 1.000  recall 0.819  false supports 0

Read the table the way chapter 12 reads its own. Every changed figure was caught (14 of 14, and none got through as supported). The five false supports are all near misses: "staff" for "visitors", "child" for "adult", "individual" for "group", "bicycle" for "car". Every content word of the claim is in the sentence except one, and 4 of 5 or 3 of 4 words clears the 0.6 bar. The eight supported claims that were marked CONTRADICTED are the true quantified ones ("can hold more than 280 visitors"): the rule sees a number that is not in the sentence and cannot do the comparison. And the ten not-enough-information claims judged otherwise include the ones that were marked CONTRADICTED because the best sentence, about a different fact of the same venue, shared the venue's name with the claim and so passed the overlap bar before the numbers failed to match. That last point deserves a moment: the venue name is counting as evidence, because it is a content word like any other. The sweep at the bottom shows what moving the bar does: raising MIN_OVERLAP to 0.9 removes every false support and costs eleven points of recall. There is no setting that fixes both, which is why the next milestones measure the judge instead of trusting it.

milestones.title: recall, precision and one support score
milestones.task: Write entails(statement, doc_ids, corpus, judge=None) (documents that do not exist are ignored; none left means False), check_statement(stmt, corpus, judge=None) returning cites (per citation: doc, status, alone, irrelevant), recall, precision (a 0/1 per citation) and support, verify_answer(answer, corpus, judge=None) returning statements and the answer's support (0.0 for an answer with no statements), and citation_report(answers, corpus, judge=None) returning the rates existence, quotes, recall, precision, uncited and the counts statements and citations. Rates with a zero denominator are 1.0, except uncited, which is 0.0.
milestones.checkpoint: python3 check.py shows this milestone as ✔. It checks entails by hand, then the six-sentence answer of chapter 12 statement by statement (recall, per-citation status, alone, irrelevant, precision, the support values and the minimum), the empty cases, the report on that answer (existence 5/6, quotations 4/6, recall 3/6, precision 3/6, one uncited), and then the full report on the dev and test sets against an independent count. Finally it checks that answers with a support above zero are right about 90% of the time and answers with support zero are wrong about 90% of the time.
milestones.explain:
Chapter 12 defines two citation metrics after Gao et al. (2023), the ALCE paper. Take one statement and the documents it cites.

Citation recall (per statement)
1 if the statement has at least one citation and the cited documents, taken together, entail it; otherwise 0. It asks whether the sentence is backed.
Citation precision (per citation)
A citation is irrelevant if its document alone does not entail the statement and the statement's other citations still do. A citation scores 1 if its statement has recall 1 and the citation is not irrelevant. It asks whether every footnote is pulling its weight; a statement that stacks four footnotes where one would do is padded, not better sourced.

These sit beside the two checks of milestone 1, which you report separately: the share of citations that point at a real source (existence) and the share whose quotation is verbatim (quotes). Four numbers, four questions. The six-sentence answer of chapter 12, with the same corpus, makes the difference vivid. This is its check by your finished functions:

from solution import *

CORP = {"1": "Harbourline Ltd reported revenue of 412 million pounds in 2025, up 8 percent from 2024. Operating profit was 61 million pounds. "
             "The company employs 3,200 people, of whom 1,100 work in Leeds. The board did not recommend a dividend for 2025. "
             "The chief executive, Mara Quince, joined in 2021.",
        "2": "Harbourline opened a second distribution centre in Doncaster in March 2025. The site cost 38 million pounds and has capacity for 90,000 parcels a day."}
ROWS = [
    ("Harbourline's revenue was 412 million pounds in 2025.", [("1", "revenue of 412 million pounds")]),
    ("Harbourline operating profit was 61 million pounds.", [("1", "Operating profit was 61 million pounds"), ("2", "capacity for 90,000 parcels")]),
    ("Harbourline paid a dividend of 12 pence.", [("1", "dividend of 12 pence")]),
    ("The Doncaster centre cost 38 million pounds.", [("2", "The site cost 38 million pounds")]),
    ("Harbourline was fined 2 million pounds by a regulator.", [("3", "fined 2 million pounds")]),
    ("Harbourline's chief executive joined in 2021.", []),
]
answer = {"statements": [{"text": t, "cites": [{"doc": d, "quote": q} for d, q in cs]} for t, cs in ROWS]}
res = verify_answer(answer, CORP)
for i, (st, (text, _)) in enumerate(zip(res["statements"], ROWS), 1):
    cites = ", ".join(f"[{c['doc']}] {c['status']}{' IRRELEVANT' if c['irrelevant'] else ''}" for c in st["cites"]) or "(no citation)"
    print(f"s{i}  recall {st['recall']}  precision {st['precision']}  support {st['support']:.2f}   {cites}")
print("answer support (the weakest statement):", res["support"])
rep = citation_report([answer], CORP)
print({k: round(v, 3) if isinstance(v, float) else v for k, v in rep.items()})

print("\nthe 600 test answers, by kind: how many pass the gate (support > 0)?")
from collections import defaultdict
tab = defaultdict(lambda: [0, 0, 0])
for a in test_set():
    s = verify_answer(a, CORPUS)["support"]
    row = tab[a["kind"]]

Statement 2 cites two sources that both exist and both quote truthfully, but the second is about parcels, not profit: recall is 1, and precision is [1, 0]. Statement 3 quotes a sentence that is not in the document (the dividend of 12 pence): quote_not_found, with the text actually contradicting it. Statement 5 cites a document that does not exist. Statement 6 is true and has no citation. The five of six citations that point at something real look like "83% citation accuracy". Only half of the statements are backed.

The second job of this milestone is the one that feeds the abstention policy. For each statement compute a support score: 0.0 unless it has citations, every citation is ok (milestone 1) and the judge says the cited documents together SUPPORT it (milestone 2), in which case it is the judge's overlap score. A single failed check zeroes the statement, which is how a hard gate behaves. The support of an answer is the minimum over its statements: an answer with four good sentences and one fabricated citation is not 80% good, it is a liability. The cross-tab at the bottom of the output above shows what that gate does to the 600 test answers by kind: every unsupported, wrong_number, fabricated and fake_quote answer is stopped (0 of 190 get through), 305 of the 334 good ones pass, and the failures that survive are the 31 near misses (of 36) and one misattributed answer. So the gate does what the chapter says a verifier should, and also what it warns about: 29 correct answers are needlessly vetoed (the quantified claims) and 32 wrong ones are stamped as checked.

milestones.title: the risk-coverage curve
milestones.task: Write risk_coverage(rows) for rows of (confidence, correct), returning [(t, coverage, risk), ...] for each distinct confidence, highest first; aurc(points) and max_coverage_at_risk(points, max_risk) (0.0 if no point qualifies). oracle_aurc is given.
milestones.checkpoint: python3 check.py shows this milestone as ✔. It checks the five-answer example above (a tie at 0.8 as one group, AURC 0.2633), the empty input, the constant-confidence case (AURC is the error rate), the coverage queries; then seeded random data: with all confidences distinct there is one point per answer and AURC is the mean of the risks after each answer; cubing the confidences changes nothing (only the ranking matters); a perfect ranking has the oracle AURC. Finally it checks, on the test set, that oracle < verifier < self-reported < no skill, that the assistant's own confidence never reaches 10% risk, and that the verifier answers more than 45% of questions at under 5% risk.
milestones.explain:
Checks tell you which answers look sound. Now suppose the system may decline. Each answer has a confidence, a number that is higher when the answer is more likely right, and the system answers when the confidence reaches a threshold t. Two quantities describe the policy (chapter 11):

Coverage
The share of all questions the system answers. Low coverage means many refusals.
Risk
The share of the answered questions that are wrong (the selective risk). It is a leading indicator of how much users can trust an answer when one is given.

Lower the threshold and coverage rises while risk, usually, rises with it, because the answers you add are the ones the signal liked least. Plot risk against coverage for every threshold and you have the risk-coverage curve. The area under it (AURC, lower is better) summarises the ranking quality of the signal in one number: a signal that put every correct answer first would keep risk at zero until coverage reached the accuracy, and one with no information would give a flat line at the overall error rate.

Two details of the computation matter. First, ties: if two answers have the same confidence, no threshold can answer one without the other, so equal confidences enter the curve together as one step. (A verifier's support score is full of ties: most good answers score exactly 1.0.) Second, the area is the sum, over the steps, of the coverage gained times the risk at that step. For a hand-worked example take five answers with confidences 0.9 (right), 0.8 (right), 0.8 (wrong), 0.5 (right) and 0.4 (wrong). The points are (0.9, coverage 0.2, risk 0), (0.8, 0.6, 1/3), (0.5, 0.8, 0.25) and (0.4, 1.0, 0.4). The 0.8 answers join in one step. AURC is 0.2×0 + 0.4×(1/3) + 0.2×0.25 + 0.2×0.4 = 0.2633.

The operational query is the third function: how much of the traffic can we answer if we will accept at most 5% wrong answers? That is max_coverage_at_risk(points, 0.05). Now compare two signals on the 600 test answers: the assistant's own confidence, and the verifier's support score from milestone 3.

from solution import *

test = test_set()
n, m = len(test), sum(a["correct"] for a in test)
support = [verify_answer(a, CORPUS)["support"] for a in test]
signals = {
    "self-reported":     [a["self_conf"] for a in test],
    "verifier support":  support,
    "support x self":    [s * a["self_conf"] for s, a in zip(support, test)],
}
print(f"{n} answers, {m} right ({m / n:.1%}).  AURC of a perfect ranking {oracle_aurc(m, n):.3f}; of no skill {1 - m / n:.3f}\n")
print(f"{'signal':<18}{'AURC':>7}{'cov @ risk<=30%':>17}{'<=10%':>8}{'<=5%':>8}{'<=2%':>8}")
for name, conf in signals.items():
    pts = risk_coverage(list(zip(conf, (a["correct"] for a in test))))
    print(f"{name:<18}{aurc(pts):>7.3f}" + "".join(f"{max_coverage_at_risk(pts, r):>{w}.1%}" for r, w in ((0.30, 17), (0.10, 8), (0.05, 8), (0.02, 8))))
600 answers, 334 right (55.7%).  AURC of a perfect ranking 0.118; of no skill 0.443

signal               AURC  cov @ risk<=30%   <=10%    <=5%    <=2%
self-reported       0.234            78.7%    0.0%    0.0%    0.0%
verifier support    0.199            56.2%   56.2%   51.8%   47.3%
support x self      0.201            56.2%   56.2%   53.5%   48.2%

Neither signal dominates. The assistant's own confidence gives a better trade at high coverage (78.7% of questions at 30% risk, against 56.2%), because the verifier can say nothing about the 44% of answers it scored zero. The verifier wins where it matters if a wrong answer is expensive: at 5% risk the assistant's own signal cannot answer anything and the verifier answers 51.8%. A common first idea is to multiply the two; here it gives an AURC of 0.201, no better than the verifier alone (0.199), because the self-reported confidence adds little where the verifier already separates good answers from bad.

milestones.title: where to put the threshold
milestones.task: Write expected_score(rows, t, penalty) (the mean over all rows; [] gives 0.0), best_threshold(rows, penalty) returning (t, score) with the tie rule and the answer-nothing case, fit_binning(rows, n_bins=10) and calibrate(conf, table). theory_threshold is given. Bin i holds confidences in [i/n, (i+1)/n); the top bin also takes 1.0; an empty bin takes its midpoint.
milestones.checkpoint: python3 check.py shows this milestone as ✔. It checks expected_score by hand (including penalty 0 and the empty list), best_threshold on four hand-worked sets (the tie rule, the answer-nothing case, an all-correct set, the empty set), the binning table by hand, and then, on seeded random data, that best_threshold really finds the best candidate with ties going upward. On the real sets it checks that for penalties 1 and 3 the chosen threshold beats answering everything by a wide margin on the test set, that the test score is not far below the calibration score, that the verifier is worth far more than the assistant's own confidence at penalty 3, and that the formula applied to recalibrated verifier support lands within 0.04 of the searched threshold.
milestones.explain:
A risk-coverage curve shows every trade; it does not choose one. The choice is about money: what does a wrong answer cost compared with an answer that was right? Score each answered question +1 if it is right and −λ if it is wrong, and each declined question 0. The penalty λ is yours to set: 1 for an internal search helper where a wrong answer costs about what a right one earns, 9 for a medical or legal assistant where one error undoes nine good answers. The expected score of a threshold t is the mean of these scores over all questions, answered or not.

If the confidences were calibrated (an answer given 80% confidence is right 80% of the time), answering would pay c − λ(1 − c) on average, which beats declining exactly when c > λ/(1 + λ). So λ = 1 gives a threshold of 0.5, λ = 3 gives 0.75, and λ = 9 gives 0.9. But the assistant's confidence is not calibrated: it is inflated, and the formula applied to it picks the wrong cut. Two remedies, and you write both:

  • Search. Try every distinct confidence as a threshold on a calibration set of answers with known outcomes, and keep the one with the best expected score (best_threshold). On a tie, take the higher threshold: when two thresholds earn the same, prefer to answer less. If no threshold earns more than 0, the best policy is to answer nothing (threshold math.inf, score 0).
  • Recalibrate, then use the formula. Fit a table that maps each confidence to the accuracy actually observed at that confidence (histogram binning, fit_binning), apply it (calibrate) and use λ/(1 + λ) on the recalibrated numbers. This gives the same sort of threshold with an explanation you can defend, and it needs no search.

Either way, the threshold must be scored on answers that were not used to choose it. A threshold picked on the questions you report is optimistic by construction, because you picked its best-looking cut (the held-out-set rule from the start of the course, as in Lab 1). Here is the whole experiment for both signals:

import math
from solution import *

cal, test = calibration_set(), test_set()
def rows(answers, signal):
    if signal == "self-reported":
        return [(a["self_conf"], a["correct"]) for a in answers]
    return [(verify_answer(a, CORPUS)["support"], a["correct"]) for a in answers]

for signal in ("self-reported", "verifier support"):
    rc, rt = rows(cal, signal), rows(test, signal)
    table = fit_binning(rc)
    print(f"--- {signal}: accuracy by confidence bin (from the calibration set)")
    print("   " + " ".join(f"{x:.2f}" for x in table))
    print(f"{'penalty':>8}{'chosen t':>10}{'calib':>8}{'test':>8}{'t=p/(1+p)':>11}{'test':>8}{'recal. test':>13}{'answer all':>12}")
    for pen in (0, 1, 3, 9):
        t, s_cal = best_threshold(rc, pen)
        th = theory_threshold(pen)
        recal = expected_score([(calibrate(c, table), ok) for c, ok in rt], th, pen)
        print(f"{pen:>8}{('none' if t == math.inf else format(t, '.3f')):>10}{s_cal:>+8.3f}{expected_score(rt, t, pen):>+8.3f}{th:>11.2f}"
              f"{expected_score(rt, th, pen):>+8.3f}{recal:>+13.3f}{expected_score(rt, -1, pen):>+12.3f}")
    print()

Read it left to right for the assistant's own confidence. At λ = 0 wrong answers cost nothing and answering everything is optimal. At λ = 1 the best cut is 0.71, not the formula's 0.5, and the formula applied to the raw confidences scores +0.200 on the test set where the searched cut scores +0.348 and the recalibrated formula +0.358. At λ = 3 the best cut is 0.83 and the policy earns +0.107 per question against −0.773 for answering everything. At λ = 9 the assistant's confidence is not good enough for any answer to pay: the policy declines everything, and the raw formula, which would still answer the questions above 0.9, loses 0.13 per question. For the verifier, a threshold near 0.86 earns +0.465 per question at λ = 3 and +0.473 at λ = 9: because a verified answer is almost always right, the price of an error hardly matters to where the line goes. The test scores differ from the calibration scores by a few hundredths in either direction; with only 600 answers, differences of that size are noise (the intervals of chapter 4 apply to a score as to any rate).
